analysis.one_liner: Speeds cheaper generic drugs to market by closing patent-listing loopholes brand-name drug makers use to delay competition.
analysis.headline: The Prescription Drug Fair Competition Act of 2002 never got a vote: it sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee from July 29, 2002 until that Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug faces a generic competitor, its maker can list new patents at the FDA and use patent lawsuits to trigger an automatic 30-month hold on the generic's approval — a tactic that can delay cheaper versions by years. This bill would require drug companies to list their patents with the FDA within 30 days of approval, take away the automatic 30-month hold for late-listed patents, strip the 180-day generic exclusivity reward from generic makers who sit on it instead of bringing their drug to market, and require courts to expedite the resulting patent disputes. It also includes protections for innovators, keeping disclosed generic manufacturing details confidential and ensuring courts don't deny injunctions just because a generic maker can pay damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone who pays for prescription drugs — households, employers, and insurers — because the bill targets the patent practices that keep lower-priced generic versions off the market for months or years after patents should have stopped blocking them [S2][S3]. Generic drug makers also gain faster pathways to approval, though the bill disciplines those who file a challenge and then delay marketing [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires brand-name companies to file all relevant patent information with the FDA within 30 days of drug approval (or patent issuance), with public publication of the key details, ending the practice of adding patents late to block generics [S2][S3].

Bars the automatic 30-month hold on generic approval for patents listed late, instead giving patent owners just 45 days to sue — and if they don't sue in that window, they lose the right to sue later over that patent [S2][S3].

Strips the valuable 180-day generic exclusivity from the first challenger if it fails to market the drug, withdraws, or engages in antitrust violations, letting the next generic applicant take the slot so a delaying challenger can't hold the market hostage [S2][S3].

Requires generic challengers to certify patent invalidity claim-by-claim when a patent covers both the drug and its uses, and lets a court deny the 30-month hold without considering whether the generic maker can afford to pay damages [S2][S3].
Directs the Federal Trade Commission to report to Congress within five years on whether the changes sped products to market and lowered drug prices, with $5 million authorized for the work [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies, which would lose the ability to list patents late and trigger automatic 30-month delays to generic approval, and lose some litigation leverage over generics. Generic makers that file a challenge and then fail to market would forfeit their exclusivity reward.

drawbacks.text: Patent owners who legitimately list patents late — for example, a patent issued just after approval through no fault of their own — would face a narrow 45-day window to sue and could be barred from infringement suits entirely if they miss deadlines, weakening valid patent rights [S2][S3].

The forfeiture rules cut both ways: a generic company that loses or settles patent litigation could lose its 180-day exclusivity, and the threat of forfeiture could deter some legitimate first challenges — though the bill's purpose is precisely to stop challengers who use that exclusivity to delay competition [S2][S3].

Courts would be required to expedite patent suits and disregard a generic applicant's ability to pay damages when deciding injunctions, shifting costs and speed demands onto the judiciary and patent holders [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core — a 30-day patent-listing deadline, no automatic 30-month hold on late-listed patents, and forfeiture of exclusivity for challengers who don't market — aims squarely at practices that keep cheaper generics off the market, which means higher drug bills for patients and insurers. The cost falls mainly on brand-name manufacturers' litigation and delay tactics, with some genuine risk to patent owners whose patents issue late. The bill preserves accommodations for innovators (confidentiality of disclosed formulations, limits on using ability-to-pay against injunctions), so it is a targeted anti-delay measure rather than a broad weakening of pharmaceutical patents.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2002 and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which passed it down to its Health subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Sherrod Brown of Ohio, joined by Rep. Henry Waxman, introduced the bill on July 26, 2002 [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day [S5].
Three days later, on July 29, 2002, it was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Health [S5].
That was the last action recorded: the bill never received a subcommittee markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: they kept the ability to list patents late, trigger automatic 30-month holds on generic approvals, and preserve their market exclusivity longer. Patients kept paying brand-name prices for longer.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 20 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill died in committee without any roll-call vote, so the record shows no test of partisan or bipartisan support.

industries.note: The bill attacks the tools these companies use to stretch exclusivity: late patent listing, automatic 30-month approval holds, and settlement-driven delay. Their gain from blocking it is prolonged monopoly pricing that consumers pay for.

Generics reach the market faster under the bill's limits on stays and clearer certification rules. The 180-day exclusivity forfeiture also disciplines generic makers who win a challenge but delay marketing, so generic companies that compete quickly benefit while those who stall lose.
